extracted.intended_audience: general newspaper readers interested in wartime developments
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and implicit standards used in wartime news reporting to assess and report the results of air raids—how destruction is verified, what counts as a successful raid, and what operational factors explain success. Focuses on photographic verification and operational metrics (planes destroyed, tonnage, targets hit, own losses).

rubrics_metrics.name: Photographic verification of raid damage (before-and-after photos)
rubrics_metrics.description: 'When the Allied air forces ... report more enemy planes destroyed on the ground, they usually have “before and after” photographs to prove it.' Photographic comparison is the basis for making ground-destruction claims official.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use previous reconnaissance photographs showing potential targets as a base; take pictures during various stages of the attack; compare before-during-after imagery to detect bomb craters and burning aircraft. A series of images (even taken a minute apart) can reveal craters or newly formed damage and allows rechecking. Anti-patterns: do not accept crew reports alone — crew reports of blasts or burning aircraft are noted but specific numbers are not added until experts examine photos. Note that poor single images can mislead; multiple timed images reduce error.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expert photo-interpretation required before counting destroyed aircraft
rubrics_metrics.description: Crew reports of bomb bursts among parked planes and blazes are recorded, but 'specific numbers are not added to the tally sheet until experts have examined before-and-after photographs.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Have trained interpreters (photo experts) compare reconnaissance and attack photographs and make final determinations about numbers destroyed. Recheck anomalies (e.g., where one picture might give rise to uncertainty) by consulting additional frames or series. Example/observation: post-raid field checks sometimes find more wrecks than originally reported, so expert interpretation and ground checks are part of the verification process.

rubrics_metrics.name: Surprise and concentration as operational criteria for effective ground attacks
rubrics_metrics.description: Allied successes against grounded aircraft are attributed to raids being carried out 'with a great degree of surprise,' catching large concentrations of enemy planes before they could be moved or adequately defended.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Operational planning should aim for surprise and rapid concentration on enemy airfields to maximize ground destruction. Indicators of effectiveness include large numbers of parked aircraft caught in one strike and minimal time for the enemy to launch protective fighters or disperse assets. Anti-pattern: dispersed or well-guarded fields with active fighter patrols reduce effectiveness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Metrics for evaluating raid success (targets hit, tonnage, enemy losses, own losses)
rubrics_metrics.description: Raid success is assessed by the degree of damage to 'important industrial and military targets and a supply ship,' tonnage of bombs delivered (e.g., 'The Liberators added 175 tons of bombs'), enemy aircraft destroyed (air combat and ground kills), and friendly losses relative to the assault's scale ('loss of 11 planes ... remarkably small in view of the large attacking forces').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Report and evaluate raids using multiple quantitative and qualitative indicators: specific strategic targets hit (docks, railroad yards, power stations, naval oil depots, seaplane bases), bomb tonnage dropped, number of enemy planes destroyed (air and ground), material damage (fires, cratered runways, disabled facilities), and friendly aircraft losses as a proportion of attacking force. Use photographic and reconnaissance confirmation for claims. Contextualize these metrics with statements on tactics/equipment to explain low or high losses (e.g., 'proof of superior tactics, equipment and leadership').
